section.title: Introduction
section.para: Numeric extraction on the document pipeline combines temporal mentions, document-date election, money amounts, measured quantities, and optional document-dated currency conversion. A dateline elects the document date and resolves the relative expressions behind it; money mentions carry normalized BigDecimal amounts and ISO currency codes; MoneyConversionAnnotator restates those amounts in one target currency as of that date. NumericPacks assembles the whole thing in one call.
All extractors are model-free: they scan the text once, without regular expressions, and every mention keeps the span it covers in the original text.

section.title: Temporal, money, and conversion
Ready-made pipelines
section.para: NumericPacks assembles the annotators for one kind of number: money(), quantity(), temporal(), and fullPipeline(), each with a Locale variant that reads a document the way its region writes and denominates numbers. The packs exist mainly for one ordering rule that is easy to get wrong: the temporal annotator elects the dateline that resolves relative expressions, so it must run before DocumentDateAnnotator. Use NumericPacks.annotators(region) when the pipeline needs more, a MoneyConversionAnnotator for instance, and add to the returned list.

section.title: Relative dates
section.para: When the date is known from metadata rather than from the text, pass it to the TemporalAnnotator(TemporalExtractor, LocalDate) constructor, or use NumericPacks.temporal(LocalDate). A fixed reference is used for every document and wins over any dateline in it.

section.title: Regional number notations
section.para: The extractors read digits in one written convention, named by NumberNotation: LATIN_US groups with commas and marks the fraction with a dot, LATIN_EU does the opposite. The choice matters by a factor of a thousand, since 1.234,56 is just over a thousand in one convention and just over one in the other. Text that cannot be read whole in the stated convention is rejected rather than approximated, so a document in the wrong notation yields no mentions instead of wrong ones.

section.title: Spelled-out currencies
section.para: The word table is deliberately short: it holds only English words that name one currency each in ordinary use. Words naming several currencies at once, such as peso, franc, and krone, are left out rather than guessed at, as is won, which is an everyday English verb. A subunit such as cents is not the currency, and a hyphen behind the word marks a compound such as euro-cent and rejects the candidate. The one knowingly ambiguous entry is pound, which also names a weight: 3 pounds of flour is read as money.

section.title: Quantities
section.para: QuantityAnnotator adds a quantity layer over the raw text, so it requires no other layer. A mention is a number with a percent marker or a unit token; a bare number is never a quantity, which also keeps money mentions out of this layer. Percentages are reported with the unit %, whether written as a sign or as the word percent. No unit conversion is performed: 2.5km keeps the value 2.5 and the unit km.
